name: Hybrid Immunity and Prior Infection Effects
anchorClaim: Individuals with both prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and vaccination (hybrid immunity) show measurably higher protection against reinfection or severe disease compared to vaccination alone, as reported in observational and cohort studies of vaccine effectiveness.
plainQuestion: Does having had a prior COVID-19 infection, on top of being vaccinated, give you extra protection against reinfection or severe disease compared to vaccination alone?
confidenceSummary: This 31% score is Preliminary because only 2 of the 45 sources are randomized trials, and just over half of the evidence supports the claim only under specific conditions, like a certain age group or virus variant, rather than as a general effect.

guide.whatScienceSays:
DATOM looked at 45 pieces of evidence for this claim. Of those, 20 (44%) directly support the idea that hybrid immunity, meaning you already had a prior infection plus a vaccine, protects you more than vaccination alone. Only 2 (4%) directly argue against that simple story. The rest, 23 pieces of evidence (51%), a slim majority, only support the claim under certain conditions: specific age groups, specific virus variants, specific vaccines, or specific time windows.

The single strongest piece of supporting evidence comes from a study that followed 101,941 people. It found that hybrid immunity cut the risk of reinfection by 26 to 36%, a real effect measured in a large group of people.

But the "it depends" evidence is where the real story is. One study followed 56 dialysis patients. Their average age was 69.1, and 76.8% of them already had a documented past infection. Before getting an updated XBB.1.5 vaccine dose, they already had detectable antibodies and immune cells in their blood. That is good evidence for how the immune system works. But it is flagged as conditional, because dialysis patients have weaker immune systems than average. What is true for them may not be true for a healthy adult.

And a survey of 535 residents in Pau da Lima, a neighborhood in Salvador, Brazil, found something important. Even though about 97% of people there already had some mix of prior infection and vaccination, a variant called BQ.1* still infected 56% of the population. That is a clear reminder: hybrid immunity lowers your risk, it does not erase it.
guide.howConfident:
DATOM gives this claim a confidence score of 31%, which falls in the "Preliminary" band. That is noticeably lower than the 44% of evidence that directly supports the claim, a 13 point gap worth pointing out directly.

Confidence is not just a vote count. It measures how strong and how consistent the evidence actually is, and on both counts, this evidence base is weaker than the 44% headline number suggests.

Only 2 of the 45 pieces of evidence are randomized controlled trials, the gold-standard study design for proving cause and effect. But both of those two studies list their sample size as "Not reported," so we cannot actually check how much statistical weight they carry. Separately, DATOM's own scoring flags 9 of the 45 pieces of evidence as too small a group to trust the result strongly.

The rest of the evidence is spread across 36 different research methods: cohort studies using blood tests, case-control studies, disease-spread models, and literature reviews. It comes from 28 different published sources and 11 different institutions. That is a wide variety of angles, but almost none of them repeat each other, so there is very little independent confirmation of any single result.

On top of that, 24 of the 45 pieces of evidence (53%), more than half, are extracted as text only, without the full original document attached. None of the 45 have their journal information on file either. That means more than half of this evidence base cannot be independently double-checked against the original document.

Put it together: a 44% support rate, built mostly on conditional findings, spread across many different methods, with more than half impossible to independently verify. That combination earns a "Preliminary" score, even though outright contradiction is rare, just 4%.
decisionSupport: The evidence leans supportive overall: 20 of the 45 pieces of evidence (44%) support added protection from hybrid immunity, versus just 2 (4%) that argue against it. The strongest example is a study of 101,941 people showing hybrid immunity cut reinfection risk by 26 to 36%. But DATOM's confidence score is well below that raw support number, at 31% ("Preliminary"), so treat the lean toward "yes" as a starting point, not a final answer.

Be cautious with the two randomized controlled trials in this set: both list their sample size as "Not reported." Randomized trials are normally the strongest kind of evidence, but here we cannot check how much statistical weight they actually carry.

More than half the evidence, 23 of 45 pieces of evidence (51%), only applies under specific conditions: a certain age group, a certain variant, or a certain time period. For example, a finding from a study of 56 dialysis patients (a group with weaker immune systems) should not be assumed to apply to healthy adults without checking whether it actually does.

Do not treat hybrid immunity as full protection. A study of 535 people in Salvador, Brazil found that the BQ.1* variant still infected 56% of the population, even though about 97% of people there already had prior infection and/or vaccination.

Before citing this in anything important, check the original sources yourself. 24 of the 45 pieces of evidence (53%) are missing their full original document, and none of the 45 have journal information on file, so the underlying study should be looked up directly rather than trusted from the extracted summary alone.
guide.faultLines:
Few Strong Trials at the Top: only 2 of the 45 pieces of evidence are randomized controlled trials, the design best suited to prove cause and effect, and both list their sample size as "Not reported." DATOM's own scoring separately flags 9 of the 45 as too small a group to trust strongly. The other 43 are spread across 36 different research methods, observational studies, computer models, and literature reviews, drawn from 28 different published sources and 11 different institutions. That variety is wide, but it means almost nothing gets independently repeated and confirmed.

Real Disagreement Isn't Settled: 23 of the 45 pieces of evidence (51%), a slim majority, only support the claim under specific conditions. That might mean a certain group of people (like dialysis patients or older adults), a certain variant (like BQ.1*), or a certain time window. So the headline 44% support number is not one clean, consistent effect. It is a patchwork of different findings for different groups that has never been fully explained or brought together into one clear picture. The 535 person study in Salvador, Brazil is a direct example. The BQ.1* variant still infected 56% of people there, despite 97% already having prior infection and/or vaccination. That has never been fully resolved against a simple "hybrid immunity protects you" story.

We Can't Always Check the Sources: 24 of the 45 pieces of evidence (53%), more than half, are text extractions without the full original document, and journal information is missing for all 45. On top of that, 25 of the 45 (56%) are dated 2026, which DATOM has confirmed is a real, recent publication date rather than a data entry error. That means most of this evidence is both hard to independently double check, and too new to have been reviewed, repeated, or cited much by other researchers yet.

datoms.claim: Dialysis patients with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection history show detectable spike-specific antibody and T-cell immunity at baseline before XBB.1.5 vaccination.
datoms.source: Saskia Bronder, Rebecca Urschel, Felix Reinhardt, Janine Mihm, Élora Schlienger "SARS-CoV-2-specific immunity after XBB.1.5 vaccination is not significantly altered by subsequent influenza vaccination in dialysis patients." (2026). doi:10.1038/s41598-026-60726-0
datoms.population: Dialysis patients (n=56, mean age 69.1 years, 76.8% with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection history)
datoms.measure: Spike-specific IgG antibodies and CD4/CD8 T-cell levels at baseline
datoms.methodology: Observational cohort study with flow cytometry and ELISA
datoms.notes: Study limited to dialysis patients; generalizability to immunocompetent populations unclear. Small sample sizes in some subgroups.

datoms.claim: Older adults vaccinated against COVID-19 generate diminished antibody production and T-cell activation compared to younger individuals, resulting in lower vaccine effectiveness.
datoms.source: Jorge G. Ruiz, Melissa K. Andrew "COVID-19 vaccination and hybrid immunity in older adults" (2023). doi:10.1016/s2666-7568(23)00112-5
datoms.population: Older adults receiving COVID-19 vaccines
datoms.measure: Vaccine effectiveness, antibody production, T-cell activation
datoms.notes: Host factors including immunosenescence and underlying health status contribute to less effective vaccine responses in older adults.

datoms.claim: Individuals with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection before November 2020 showed reduced risk of RT-PCR-detected BQ.1* infection compared to those without such early prior exposure.
datoms.source: Juan P. Aguilar Ticona, Meng Xiao, Dan Li, Nívison Nery, Matt D. T. Hitchings "Extensive transmission of SARS-CoV-2 BQ.1* variant in a population with high levels of hybrid immunity: A prevalence survey" (2023). doi:10.1016/j.ijid.2023.11.039
datoms.population: 535 residents of Pau da Lima, Salvador, Brazil with documented prior SARS-CoV-2 exposure history from November 2020 onwards
datoms.measure: Risk of RT-PCR-detected BQ.1* infection stratified by timing of prior infection
datoms.methodology: Cohort study with logistic regression analysis
datoms.notes: Misclassification in identification of prior SARS-CoV-2 exposure using serosurveys due to inability to distinguish vaccination-induced from infection-induced seropositivity.

datoms.claim: Individuals with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection plus vaccination (hybrid immunity) produce measurably higher neutralizing antibody levels compared to vaccination alone, six months after booster vaccination.
datoms.source: Amy May Lin Quek, Suqing Wang, Ooiean Teng, Bhuvaneshwari D O Shunmuganathan, B. Er "Hybrid immunity augments cross-variant protection against COVID-19 among immunocompromised individuals" (2024). doi:10.1016/j.jinf.2024.106238
datoms.population: Patients with autoimmune diseases, chronic comorbidities, and healthy controls; infected vs. non-infected participants
datoms.measure: Neutralizing antibody levels to wild-type SARS-CoV-2 and variants (Beta, Gamma, Delta, Omicron)
datoms.sample_size: 519 total participants (137 autoimmune, 153 multimorbidity, 229 healthy); 2,390 unvaccinated infected controls
datoms.notes: The study focuses on serological measures (neutralizing antibodies) rather than clinical outcomes of reinfection or severe disease.

datoms.claim: The dominance of sequential infection pathways for COVID-19 transmission is robust across variations in model structure and relative pathogen transmissibility, with sequential sources accounting for 37.1% to 75.5% of COVID-19 incidence across tested scenarios.
datoms.source: Mani Dhakal, Brajendra K Singh, Rajeev K Azad "Infection History Shapes Co-Epidemic Dynamics: A Transmission Source-Pathway Decomposition for COVID-19 and Influenza." (2026). doi:10.3390/microorganisms14061239
datoms.population: Homogeneously mixing population in co-epidemic model
datoms.domain: Mathematical epidemiology; COVID-19 and influenza co-circulation
datoms.measure: Proportion of COVID-19 incidence attributable to sequential infection pathway across model variants
datoms.methodology: Deterministic compartmental co-infection model with sensitivity analysis across model structures and transmissibility scenarios
datoms.notes: The model assumes homogeneous mixing and equal R0 baseline for comparability. While precise percentages vary with alternative assumptions, the qualitative conclusions about infection sequence mattering are robust across tested frameworks.

datoms.claim: Individuals with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection who receive mRNA vaccination show lower hospitalization rates compared to those vaccinated without prior infection.
datoms.source: Lucy L. Li, Chunlei Zheng, Jennifer La, Nhan V. Do, Paul A. Monach "Impact of prior SARS-CoV-2 infection on incidence of hospitalization and adverse events following mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccination: A nationwide, retrospective cohort study" (2022). doi:10.1016/j.vaccine.2022.01.026
datoms.population: US adults receiving mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccination with and without prior infection history
datoms.measure: Hospitalization incidence following mRNA vaccination
datoms.notes: Retrospective design; potential unmeasured confounding; reliance on documented infection records which may underestimate prior infection prevalence.

datoms.claim: Vaccine effectiveness studies typically do not account for behavioral changes induced by knowledge of vaccine protection, which may increase pathogen exposure and reduce measured vaccine effectiveness.
datoms.source: Bronner P Gonçalves, Piero L Olliaro, Sheena G Sullivan, Benjamin J Cowling "Natural direct effects of vaccines and post-vaccination behaviour." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.128888
datoms.population: Vaccinated individuals in observational and cohort vaccine effectiveness studies
datoms.measure: Vaccine effectiveness estimates accounting for behavioral mediation
datoms.notes: This is a conceptual paper without empirical data collection or analysis. It does not provide quantitative estimates of the magnitude of behavioral confounding in existing vaccine effectiveness studies.

datoms.claim: COVID-19 vaccination reduces cumulative incidence of COVID-19 in a co-epidemic setting by disrupting sequential transmission pathways.
datoms.source: Mani Dhakal, Brajendra K Singh, Rajeev K Azad "Infection History Shapes Co-Epidemic Dynamics: A Transmission Source-Pathway Decomposition for COVID-19 and Influenza." (2026). doi:10.3390/microorganisms14061239
datoms.population: Homogeneously mixing population in co-epidemic model
datoms.domain: Mathematical epidemiology; COVID-19 and influenza co-circulation
datoms.measure: Cumulative incidence of COVID-19 (fraction of population infected over 180 days)
datoms.notes: The model assumes homogeneous mixing and does not incorporate country-specific demographic data, age structure, or gender differences in susceptibility.

datoms.claim: COVID-19 vaccination (two or more doses) is not associated with increased risk of acute myocardial infarction in young adults.
datoms.source: Tarun Bhatnagar, Janani Surya Ravichandran, Jeyashree Kathiresan, Manickam Ponnaiah, Hari Krishan Aggarwal "Factors associated with thrombotic events among young adults in India, 2021-23: A multi-centric hospital-based matched case -control study." (2026). doi:10.25259/IJMR_2949_2025
datoms.population: Young adults aged 18-45 years hospitalized with thrombotic events in India
datoms.measure: Association between COVID-19 vaccination and acute myocardial infarction risk
datoms.sample_size: 432 cases with acute myocardial infarction and 1,293 matched controls
datoms.notes: The study was conducted during a period of widespread SARS-CoV-2 infection, which may have affected the ability to isolate vaccination effects.

datoms.claim: Individuals with hybrid immunity (prior MPXV infection plus MVA-BN vaccination) show higher magnitude of B6R-specific CD4+ T-cell responses than those with vaccination alone.
datoms.source: David da Fonseca Araújo, Christoph Schultheiß, Leon Cords, Hendrik Karsten, Robin Woost "MPXV H3L elicits broadly directed CD4 T cell responses in mpox patients and MVA vaccinees." (2026). doi:10.1038/s44298-026-00205-5
datoms.population: Mpox-infected individuals stratified by MVA-BN vaccination history: 6 with prior MVA-BN vaccination, 9 without
datoms.measure: Number of B6R-specific CD4+ T-cell responses per individual
datoms.methodology: Cohort study with peptide stimulation and intracellular cytokine staining
datoms.notes: Small subgroup sizes (n=6 hybrid immunity, n=9 infection-only); exclusively male cohort; cross-sectional design limits temporal inference.

datoms.claim: HLA-A*03:01 carriage is associated with reduced breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infection risk after vaccination.
datoms.source: Anshika Srivastava, Demetra S M Chatzileontiadou, Anurag Adhikari, Rayo Suseno, Sean Lin "COVID-19 Vaccine Reactogenicity Marks an Innate Inflammatory Response Associated With HLA Variation and Enhanced Protection." (2026). doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10085252/v1
datoms.population: 57,938 vaccinated individuals across ancestries; subset with complete vaccination and infection date information
datoms.measure: Breakthrough infection (BTI) risk in vaccinated individuals
datoms.sample_size: 57,938 total vaccinated; 47,711 with complete date information after exclusions
datoms.notes: Self-reported infection dates and breakthrough infection status. Modest effect size.

datoms.claim: Individuals with hybrid immunity have a higher probability of detectable cellular immune response (reactive IGRA) compared to those with natural immunity alone.
datoms.source: Tobias Rothoeft, Claudia S. Maier, A Talarico, Armin Hoffmann, Anne Schlegtendal "Natural and hybrid immunity after SARS-CoV-2 infection in children and adolescents" (2024). doi:10.1007/s15010-024-02225-w
datoms.population: 72 children and adolescents (aged 4-21 years) with PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection; 37 with hybrid immunity (prior infection plus BNT162b2 vaccination), 35 with natural immunity only
datoms.measure: Reactive interferon-γ release assay (IGRA) indicating cellular immune response
datoms.methodology: Cohort study with QuantiFERON-SARS-CoV-2 interferon-γ release assay
datoms.sample_size: 71 participants (one excluded due to lack of material for IGRA)
datoms.notes: Relatively small sample size; all infections occurred during Omicron era; IGRA may have lower sensitivity in detecting T cell responses in younger children due to higher percentage of naive T cells; different vaccination rates between age groups prevent full comparison.

datoms.claim: Vaccination with rBCG/rChimera+Alum induces T cell-mediated protection against SARS-CoV-2 variants (Wuhan and JN.1) that is independent of neutralizing antibodies.
datoms.source: Fábio Mambelli, Alba M Gimenez, Ana Carolina V S C de Araujo, Karla K S Ramos, Jéssica P Farias "T cell-associated immunity induced by heterologous recombinant BCG and purified protein vaccination confers cross-variant protection against SARS-CoV-2." (2026). doi:10.1080/21645515.2026.2697392
datoms.population: K18-hACE2 transgenic mice, including B cell-deficient, CD4+ T cell-deficient, CD8+ T cell-deficient, and IFN-γ knockout variants
datoms.measure: Viral load reduction and cross-protection against JN.1 variant
datoms.methodology: Knockout mouse model with viral challenge
datoms.notes: Study conducted in transgenic mouse models with hACE2 expression; findings may not directly translate to human immune responses.

datoms.claim: Prior SARS-CoV-2 vaccination is associated with earlier nasal Type II interferon initiation, which correlates with reduced viral replication during naturally acquired infection.
datoms.source: Alexander Viloria Winnett, Alexandra Tabachnikova, Jonathan Chen, Kerrie Greene, Anna E Romano "Early Mucosal Type II Interferon Limits SARS-CoV-2 Replication in Humans." (2026). doi:10.64898/2026.06.29.26356894
datoms.population: 16 individuals with naturally acquired SARS-CoV-2 infection and 16 age-, sex-, and vaccination-matched uninfected individuals
datoms.measure: Viral load by RT-qPCR and Type II interferon expression by mRNA sequencing in upper respiratory sites
datoms.methodology: Longitudinal cohort study with paired-site sampling
datoms.notes: Small sample size (n=16 infected individuals); temporal and anatomical antiviral dynamics require longitudinal paired-site sampling which may limit generalizability.

datoms.claim: Among immunocompromised individuals, hybrid immunity (prior infection plus vaccination) provides cross-variant protection against COVID-19.
datoms.source: Amy May Lin Quek, Suqing Wang, Ooiean Teng, Bhuvaneshwari D O Shunmuganathan, B. Er "Hybrid immunity augments cross-variant protection against COVID-19 among immunocompromised individuals" (2024). doi:10.1016/j.jinf.2024.106238
datoms.population: Immunocompromised individuals including patients with autoimmune diseases and chronic comorbidities
datoms.measure: Neutralizing antibody levels and cross-variant serological immunity
datoms.notes: The study measures serological immunity (neutralizing antibodies) rather than clinical outcomes of reinfection or severe disease.

datoms.claim: Children aged 5-11 years with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection who receive a single dose of BNT162b2 vaccine show non-inferior immunogenicity compared to a two-dose primary vaccination regimen.
datoms.source: Cristina Prat-Aymerich, Lusine Yeghiazaryan, Rishi Delan Pathirana, Virginie Gautier, Alejandro Abner Garcia Leon "A prematurely terminated phase 2, randomised trial to evaluate immunogenicity and reactogenicity of a single versus two-dose primary vaccination regimen of the mRNA vaccine BNT162b2 in previously SARS-CoV-2 infected children 5-11 years old (CoVacc trial)." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.128769
datoms.population: Children aged 5-11 years with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection
datoms.measure: Immunogenicity (antibody response); safety and reactogenicity
datoms.notes: The trial was prematurely terminated, preventing completion of the planned immunogenicity and safety comparisons. The open-label design may introduce bias.

datoms.claim: Individuals with hybrid immunity (prior SARS-CoV-2 infection plus vaccination) demonstrate higher protection against reinfection or severe COVID-19 disease compared to vaccination alone.
datoms.source: Grace Roberts, Lena Glaser "Hybrid immunity: a combination of vaccination and prior infection probably offers the best protection against COVID" (2022). doi:10.64628/ab.vr6h9u7rw
datoms.population: Individuals with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and vaccination history
datoms.measure: Protection against reinfection or severe COVID-19 disease
datoms.notes: As a review article, the paper synthesizes existing evidence rather than presenting primary data; specific quantitative effect sizes and population details are not provided in the available text.

datoms.claim: Individuals with lysosomal disorders show measurably higher risk of COVID-19 hospitalization compared to matched controls without lysosomal disorders.
datoms.source: Blake K Byer, Zachary Butzin-Dozier, Brenda M McGrath, Joseph Muenzer, Lorne Clarke "Differential COVID-19 Outcomes Across Lysosomal Disorders." (2026). doi:10.64898/2026.06.22.26356274
datoms.population: 5,460 patients with lysosomal disorders and 10,920 matched controls from U.S. electronic health records
datoms.measure: Odds of COVID-19 hospitalization
datoms.notes: The study does not report limitations explicitly in the provided abstract and results sections.

datoms.claim: Hybrid immunity provides measurably higher protection against severe Omicron disease compared to vaccination alone or unvaccinated status.
datoms.source: Joshua Nealon, Yonatan M. Mefsin, Martina McMenamin, Kylie E. C. Ainslie, Benjamin J. Cowling "Reported effectiveness of COVID-19 monovalent booster vaccines and hybrid immunity against mild and severe Omicron disease in adults: A systematic review and meta-regression analysis" (2024). doi:10.1016/j.jvacx.2024.100451
datoms.population: Adults with hybrid immunity or third/fourth mRNA COVID-19 monovalent vaccine doses against Omicron
datoms.domain: Infectious disease epidemiology; COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness
datoms.measure: Vaccine effectiveness (VE) against severe Omicron disease
datoms.sample_size: 55 eligible studies reporting 269 VE estimates; 48 (18%) describing hybrid immunity
datoms.notes: Limited data specifically on hybrid immunity (18% of estimates); most estimates from test-negative design studies; data collection ended 31 December 2022.

datoms.claim: Spike-specific IgG antibodies and CD4 T-cell levels remain significantly elevated 6 months after XBB.1.5 vaccination compared to unvaccinated dialysis patients.
datoms.source: Saskia Bronder, Rebecca Urschel, Felix Reinhardt, Janine Mihm, Élora Schlienger "SARS-CoV-2-specific immunity after XBB.1.5 vaccination is not significantly altered by subsequent influenza vaccination in dialysis patients." (2026). doi:10.1038/s41598-026-60726-0
datoms.population: Dialysis patients vaccinated with XBB.1.5 (n=18 at 6-month follow-up) compared to unvaccinated dialysis patients (n=23) recruited in same period
datoms.measure: Spike-specific IgG antibodies and CD4 T-cell levels at 6 months post-vaccination
datoms.methodology: Observational cohort study with longitudinal follow-up
datoms.notes: Relatively small sample size for 6-month follow-up (n=18 vaccinated, n=23 unvaccinated). Two patients lost to follow-up (1 death, 1 transplant).

datoms.claim: Dirty mice co-housed with pet store mice show reduced serum spike-binding antibody titers after prime mRNA vaccination compared to specific-pathogen-free mice.
datoms.source: Beatriz Praena, Frances K Shepherd, Cera A McDonald, Devyani Joshi, Sneh Lata Gupta "Dirty mice better recapitulate key features of mRNA vaccine immunogenicity observed in humans." (2026). doi:10.1128/mbio.00983-26
datoms.population: Laboratory mice co-housed with pet store mice (dirty mice) versus specific-pathogen-free mice
datoms.measure: Serum spike-binding antibody titers post-prime vaccination
datoms.notes: The paper does not explicitly state limitations but focuses on demonstrating the dirty mouse model as a screening tool prior to human trials.

datoms.claim: Individuals with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection demonstrate greater protection against reinfection than vaccination alone.
datoms.source: "Having SARS-CoV-2 once confers much greater immunity than a vaccine, but vaccination remains vital" (2021). doi:10.1126/science.abm1207
datoms.population: Individuals with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to vaccinated individuals
datoms.measure: Protection against reinfection or severe disease
datoms.notes: Specific limitations are not detailed in the provided text.

datoms.claim: A reduced homologous booster dose of BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine maintains immunogenicity comparable to standard dosing.
datoms.source: Stéphanie Depickère, Pieter Pannus, Sarah Houben, Alexia Charles, Leo Heyndrickx "Safety and immunogenicity of a reduced, homologous booster dose of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine: a single blind, randomized, non-inferiority follow-up trial." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.128897
datoms.population: Individuals receiving BNT162b2 booster vaccination
datoms.measure: Immunogenicity and safety of reduced-dose booster
datoms.notes: The provided text is limited to the introduction and rationale; full results, limitations, and detailed methodology are not included in the excerpt.

datoms.claim: Individuals carrying HLA-A*03:01 who report stronger vaccine side effects exhibit reduced risk of breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infection independent of HLA genotype.
datoms.source: Anshika Srivastava, Demetra S M Chatzileontiadou, Anurag Adhikari, Rayo Suseno, Sean Lin "COVID-19 Vaccine Reactogenicity Marks an Innate Inflammatory Response Associated With HLA Variation and Enhanced Protection." (2026). doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10085252/v1
datoms.population: 50,535 vaccinated individuals self-identified as White, plus replication cohort of 4,575 individuals; U.S.-based NMDP bone marrow donors
datoms.measure: Breakthrough infection risk and COVID-19 symptom burden in infected individuals
datoms.sample_size: 50,535 participants in discovery cohort; 4,575 in replication cohort
datoms.notes: Self-reported side effects and infection history subject to recall bias. Primarily White ancestry cohort limits generalizability.

datoms.claim: Individuals with hybrid immunity have a higher probability of detectable neutralizing antibodies compared to those with natural immunity alone.
datoms.source: Tobias Rothoeft, Claudia S. Maier, A Talarico, Armin Hoffmann, Anne Schlegtendal "Natural and hybrid immunity after SARS-CoV-2 infection in children and adolescents" (2024). doi:10.1007/s15010-024-02225-w
datoms.population: 71 children and adolescents (aged 4-21 years) with PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection; 37 with hybrid immunity, 34 with natural immunity only
datoms.measure: Presence and titers of neutralizing antibodies (RLU)
datoms.methodology: Cohort study with VSV pseudovirus-based neutralization assay
datoms.sample_size: 71 participants (one excluded due to lack of material)
datoms.notes: Relatively small sample size; all infections occurred during Omicron era; assays validated for wild-type virus may underestimate neutralization capacity against Omicron; cannot determine whether higher neutralization is due to vaccination, age, or both.

datoms.claim: Individuals with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection show persistent IgG antibody responses measurable over 3-4 months.
datoms.source: Reshmi Dassaye, Terusha Chetty, Brodie Daniels, Trisha Ramraj, Samkelisiwe Buthelezi "Longitudinal SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence among learners, parents, and teachers in a South African school community." (2026). doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1770703
datoms.population: School community participants: learners (n=203), parents (n=71), teachers (n=18) in South Africa
datoms.measure: Persistence of SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies from baseline to follow-up
datoms.methodology: Longitudinal cohort study with paired serological testing
datoms.notes: The qualitative serological assay cannot differentiate antibodies from natural infection versus vaccination. The study lacks quantitative antibody measurements or assessment of antibody functionality.

datoms.claim: Individuals with hybrid immunity (prior MPXV infection plus MVA-BN vaccination) show broader B6R-specific CD4+ T-cell responses compared to those with infection alone.
datoms.source: David da Fonseca Araújo, Christoph Schultheiß, Leon Cords, Hendrik Karsten, Robin Woost "MPXV H3L elicits broadly directed CD4 T cell responses in mpox patients and MVA vaccinees." (2026). doi:10.1038/s44298-026-00205-5
datoms.population: 28 adult males: 15 with mpox history (6 with additional MVA-BN vaccination), 7 MVA-BN-only vaccinees, 6 unexposed controls
datoms.measure: Breadth of B6R-specific CD4+ T-cell responses (number of reactive peptides)
datoms.methodology: Cohort study with peptide stimulation and flow cytometry
datoms.notes: Small sample size (n=28); exclusively male cohort; limited temporal data on vaccination-to-infection intervals; TCR sequencing performed on only 8 individuals due to material constraints.

datoms.claim: Individuals with documented prior SARS-CoV-2 exposure and vaccination (hybrid immunity) had lower odds of BQ.1* infection compared to those without both exposures, but the difference was not statistically significant.
datoms.source: Juan P. Aguilar Ticona, Meng Xiao, Dan Li, Nívison Nery, Matt D. T. Hitchings "Extensive transmission of SARS-CoV-2 BQ.1* variant in a population with high levels of hybrid immunity: A prevalence survey" (2023). doi:10.1016/j.ijid.2023.11.039
datoms.population: 535 residents of Pau da Lima, Salvador, Brazil; 79 SARS-CoV-2 positive, 456 negative
datoms.measure: Prevalence of BQ.1* infection stratified by hybrid immunity status (prior exposure and vaccination)
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional prevalence survey with chi-square test
datoms.notes: Misclassification in identification of prior SARS-CoV-2 exposure due to inability to distinguish vaccination-induced from infection-induced seropositivity after vaccines became available.

datoms.claim: COVID-19 vaccines and boosters reduce infection and mortality in populations.
datoms.source: Fulya Ipek-Erdem, Esra Erpek, Volkan Genç, Aybars Bars, Sabri Erdem "Socioeconomic determinants of COVID-19 vaccination and mortality: a cross-national path analysis." (2026). doi:10.1186/s12889-026-28293-1
datoms.population: Population-level across multiple nations
datoms.measure: Infection rates and mortality outcomes
datoms.methodology: Literature review and cross-national path analysis
datoms.notes: The paper does not measure or compare hybrid immunity (prior infection plus vaccination) against vaccination alone, which is the specific outcome variable in the nucleus claim.

datoms.claim: Children with mRNA vaccination followed by breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infection develop enhanced Th1 responses and enriched CD4+ IFN-γ+IL10+ Spike-specific T cells, characteristic of hybrid immunity.
datoms.source: Martin Qui, Smrithi Hariharaputran, Shou Kit Hang, Jinyan Zhang, Chee Wah Tan "T cell hybrid immunity against SARS-CoV-2 in children: a longitudinal study" (2024). doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2024.105203
datoms.population: mRNA-vaccinated children aged 5-11 years who experienced breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infection
datoms.measure: Magnitude and cytokine profile of antigen-specific T cell responses (Th1, CD4+ IFN-γ+IL10+ cells)
datoms.methodology: Prospective longitudinal cohort study with cytokine release assays and intracellular cytokine staining
datoms.sample_size: 29 participants enrolled; 26 participants followed for at least 12 months with breakthrough infection; 159 blood samples analyzed
datoms.notes: Study limited to pediatric population aged 5-11; relatively small sample size (n=29 enrolled, n=26 completed); specific quantitative comparisons to vaccination-alone controls not explicitly reported.

datoms.claim: Hybrid immunity (prior SARS-CoV-2 infection plus vaccination) is present at widespread levels in populations transitioning to endemic COVID-19 phases.
datoms.source: Xueyin Mei, Sidu Feng, Wanrong Xie, Yi Sun, Liqing Wang "A population-based retrospective machine learning study of COVID-19 severity using integrated clinical and viral genomic data in Jiangsu Province, China." (2026). doi:10.1186/s12866-026-05360-6
datoms.population: Residents of Jiangsu Province, China during endemic COVID-19 phase
datoms.measure: Presence and prevalence of hybrid immunity in population
datoms.notes: The authors note that hybrid immunity is now a defining feature of endemic COVID-19 populations, necessitating region-specific approaches to understanding severe disease determinants.

datoms.claim: Cumulative incidence of COVID-19 is lowest among individuals with both prior infection and vaccination compared to other groups.
datoms.source: Abinash Virk, Matthew G. Johnson, Daniel Roellinger, Christopher G. Scott, Priya Sampathkumar "Hybrid Immunity Provides Protective Advantage Over Vaccination or Prior Remote Coronavirus Disease 2019 Alone" (2023). doi:10.1093/ofid/ofad161
datoms.population: Vaccinated and unvaccinated patients of all ages with and without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection
datoms.measure: Cumulative incidence of COVID-19 infection
datoms.methodology: Retrospective cohort study with Simon-Makuch hazard plots
datoms.sample_size: 101,941 individuals with at least 1 COVID-19 PCR test
datoms.notes: The study was conducted during a specific time period and may not capture longer-term protection or protection against newer variants.

datoms.claim: Individuals with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and mRNA vaccination show 26-36% reduction in reinfection risk compared to previously infected individuals without vaccination.
datoms.source: Abinash Virk, Matthew G. Johnson, Daniel Roellinger, Christopher G. Scott, Priya Sampathkumar "Hybrid Immunity Provides Protective Advantage Over Vaccination or Prior Remote Coronavirus Disease 2019 Alone" (2023). doi:10.1093/ofid/ofad161
datoms.population: Vaccinated and unvaccinated patients of all ages with and without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection
datoms.measure: Reinfection risk reduction (hazard ratio)
datoms.methodology: Retrospective cohort study with multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression
datoms.sample_size: 101,941 individuals with at least 1 COVID-19 PCR test
datoms.notes: The study was conducted during a specific time period (December 2020 to March 2022) and may not capture longer-term protection or protection against newer variants beyond Omicron.

datoms.claim: HLA-A*03:01 carriage is associated with higher anti-Spike IgG antibody levels after COVID-19 vaccination.
datoms.source: Anshika Srivastava, Demetra S M Chatzileontiadou, Anurag Adhikari, Rayo Suseno, Sean Lin "COVID-19 Vaccine Reactogenicity Marks an Innate Inflammatory Response Associated With HLA Variation and Enhanced Protection." (2026). doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10085252/v1
datoms.population: 156 healthcare workers receiving two doses of Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine; stratified by anti-Spike IgG levels
datoms.measure: Anti-Spike IgG antibody levels post-vaccination
datoms.sample_size: 156 healthcare workers (Group I: 50, Group II: 53, Group III: 53)
datoms.notes: Small sample size (N=156) limits generalizability. Single vaccine platform (Pfizer) and single timepoint (post-dose 2) assessed.

datoms.claim: Individuals with sequential infection history (prior influenza followed by COVID-19) account for approximately 73% of COVID-19 transmission and 76% of COVID-19 disease burden in a co-epidemic model.
datoms.source: Mani Dhakal, Brajendra K Singh, Rajeev K Azad "Infection History Shapes Co-Epidemic Dynamics: A Transmission Source-Pathway Decomposition for COVID-19 and Influenza." (2026). doi:10.3390/microorganisms14061239
datoms.population: Homogeneously mixing population in co-epidemic model
datoms.domain: Mathematical epidemiology; COVID-19 and influenza co-circulation
datoms.measure: Proportion of COVID-19 incidence and disease burden attributable to sequentially infected source population
datoms.methodology: Deterministic compartmental co-infection model simulation with source-pathway decomposition
datoms.notes: The model assumes homogeneous mixing and does not incorporate age structure, geographic variation, or behavioral differences in contact patterns.

datoms.claim: Hybrid immunity (prior infection plus vaccination) produces higher SARS-CoV-2 IgG seroprevalence than vaccination alone or infection alone.
datoms.source: Reshmi Dassaye, Terusha Chetty, Brodie Daniels, Trisha Ramraj, Samkelisiwe Buthelezi "Longitudinal SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence among learners, parents, and teachers in a South African school community." (2026). doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1770703
datoms.population: Parents (n=71) and teachers (n=18) in a South African school community; learners (n=203) in grades 1-7
datoms.measure: SARS-CoV-2 IgG seroprevalence (antibody detection via point-of-care test)
datoms.methodology: Longitudinal cohort study with serological testing
datoms.notes: The qualitative serological assay cannot differentiate antibodies arising from natural infection versus vaccination, preventing determination of the relative contribution of each source to observed seroprevalence.

datoms.claim: Sequential XBB.1.5 vaccination followed by influenza vaccination does not reduce spike-specific antibody or T-cell responses compared to XBB.1.5 vaccination alone in dialysis patients.
datoms.source: Saskia Bronder, Rebecca Urschel, Felix Reinhardt, Janine Mihm, Élora Schlienger "SARS-CoV-2-specific immunity after XBB.1.5 vaccination is not significantly altered by subsequent influenza vaccination in dialysis patients." (2026). doi:10.1038/s41598-026-60726-0
datoms.population: Dialysis patients receiving sequential XBB.1.5/influenza vaccination (n=28) compared to XBB.1.5 alone (n=17) and influenza alone (n=11)
datoms.measure: Spike-specific IgG antibodies and CD4/CD8 T-cell levels post-vaccination
datoms.methodology: Observational cohort study with comparative analysis
datoms.sample_size: 56 participants total (28 sequential, 17 XBB only, 11 Flu only)
datoms.notes: Study limited to dialysis patients; results may not generalize to immunocompetent populations. Relatively small sample sizes in individual groups.

datoms.claim: Individuals with hybrid immunity (prior SARS-CoV-2 infection plus vaccination) have significantly higher spike protein antibody titers compared to those with natural immunity alone.
datoms.source: Tobias Rothoeft, Claudia S. Maier, A Talarico, Armin Hoffmann, Anne Schlegtendal "Natural and hybrid immunity after SARS-CoV-2 infection in children and adolescents" (2024). doi:10.1007/s15010-024-02225-w
datoms.population: 72 children and adolescents (aged 4-21 years) with PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection; 37 with hybrid immunity (prior infection plus BNT162b2 vaccination), 35 with natural immunity only
datoms.measure: Spike protein-specific antibody titers (BAU/ml)
datoms.methodology: Cohort study with cross-sectional antibody measurement
datoms.notes: Relatively small sample size; all but one infection occurred during Omicron era in early 2022, limiting generalizability to other variants; assays validated for wild-type virus may not fully capture Omicron-specific responses.

datoms.claim: Hybrid immunity (prior infection plus vaccination) induces higher frequencies of pan-endemic-coronavirus-reactive T cells compared to vaccination alone across all age groups.
datoms.source: Lucie Loyal, Julian Braun, Ulf Reimer, Lil Meyer-Arndt, Larissa Henze "Hybrid immunity-based induction of durable pan-endemic-coronavirus immunity in the elderly" (2025). doi:10.1016/j.celrep.2025.115314
datoms.population: Elderly individuals and mixed age groups with varying vaccination and infection histories
datoms.measure: Frequency and functional avidity of pan-human endemic coronavirus (PHEC)-reactive T cells
datoms.methodology: Observational cohort study with peptide pool-based T cell assay
datoms.notes: The paper does not explicitly report clinical outcomes (reinfection or severe disease rates) but instead measures T cell immunogenicity as a mechanistic proxy for protection.

datoms.claim: Prior SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with protection against symptomatic reinfection.
datoms.source: Aidan T. Hanrath, Brendan A.I. Payne, Christopher J.A. Duncan "Prior SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with protection against symptomatic reinfection" (2021). doi:10.1016/j.jinf.2020.12.023
datoms.population: Healthcare workers with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection
datoms.measure: Protection against symptomatic reinfection
datoms.notes: The study does not stratify results by vaccination status, making it impossible to compare hybrid immunity (prior infection plus vaccination) to vaccination alone as the nucleus claim requires.

datoms.claim: COVID-19 vaccination (two or more doses) is not associated with increased risk of any thrombotic event in young adults.
datoms.source: Tarun Bhatnagar, Janani Surya Ravichandran, Jeyashree Kathiresan, Manickam Ponnaiah, Hari Krishan Aggarwal "Factors associated with thrombotic events among young adults in India, 2021-23: A multi-centric hospital-based matched case -control study." (2026). doi:10.25259/IJMR_2949_2025
datoms.population: Young adults aged 18-45 years hospitalized with thrombotic events in India
datoms.measure: Association between COVID-19 vaccination and any thrombotic event risk
datoms.sample_size: 767 cases with any thrombotic event and 2,144 matched controls
datoms.notes: The study was conducted during a period of widespread SARS-CoV-2 infection, which may have affected the ability to isolate vaccination effects.

datoms.claim: Hybrid immunity (prior SARS-CoV-2 infection plus vaccination) provides measurably higher protection against mild Omicron disease compared to vaccination alone or unvaccinated status.
datoms.source: Joshua Nealon, Yonatan M. Mefsin, Martina McMenamin, Kylie E. C. Ainslie, Benjamin J. Cowling "Reported effectiveness of COVID-19 monovalent booster vaccines and hybrid immunity against mild and severe Omicron disease in adults: A systematic review and meta-regression analysis" (2024). doi:10.1016/j.jvacx.2024.100451
datoms.population: Adults with hybrid immunity or third/fourth mRNA COVID-19 monovalent vaccine doses against Omicron
datoms.domain: Infectious disease epidemiology; COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness
datoms.measure: Vaccine effectiveness (VE) against mild and severe Omicron disease
datoms.notes: Limited data available specifically on hybrid immunity (only 18% of estimates); most estimates derived from test-negative design studies; data collection ended 31 December 2022.

datoms.claim: Individuals reporting vaccine side effects show reduced total SARS-CoV-2 infection burden, including fewer reinfections, compared to those without side effects.
datoms.source: Anshika Srivastava, Demetra S M Chatzileontiadou, Anurag Adhikari, Rayo Suseno, Sean Lin "COVID-19 Vaccine Reactogenicity Marks an Innate Inflammatory Response Associated With HLA Variation and Enhanced Protection." (2026). doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10085252/v1
datoms.population: 50,535 vaccinated individuals in discovery cohort; 43,527 with no or single infection; 7,008 with repeated reinfections
datoms.measure: Repeated SARS-CoV-2 reinfection (two or more infections vs. zero or one infection)
datoms.sample_size: 50,535 discovery cohort participants; 43,527 never infected or single infection; 7,008 with repeated reinfections
datoms.notes: Self-reported infection history subject to recall bias. Cross-sectional analysis cannot establish temporal causality.

datoms.claim: Hybrid immunity (prior infection plus vaccination) provides measurably higher protection against BA.5 infection compared to vaccination alone over an 8-month period.
datoms.source: João Malato, Ruy M. Ribeiro, Eugénia Fernandes, Pedro Pinto Leite, Pedro Casaca "Stability of hybrid versus vaccine immunity against BA.5 infection over 8 months" (2023). doi:10.1016/s1473-3099(22)00833-7
datoms.population: Individuals with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and vaccination versus vaccinated-only individuals
datoms.measure: Protection against BA.5 infection over 8 months
datoms.notes: Study limitations regarding generalizability to other variants or populations not fully detailed in title and abstract.

datoms.claim: In a population with high hybrid immunity (97% with prior infection and/or vaccination), the BQ.1* variant achieved 56% cumulative incidence over 5 weeks, demonstrating that hybrid immunity did not prevent widespread transmission.
datoms.source: Juan P. Aguilar Ticona, Meng Xiao, Dan Li, Nívison Nery, Matt D. T. Hitchings "Extensive transmission of SARS-CoV-2 BQ.1* variant in a population with high levels of hybrid immunity: A prevalence survey" (2023). doi:10.1016/j.ijid.2023.11.039
datoms.population: 535 residents of Pau da Lima, Salvador, Brazil, aged 2 years and older; 54% with documented prior SARS-CoV-2 exposure, 74% vaccinated
datoms.measure: Cumulative incidence of PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 BQ.1* infection
datoms.methodology: Population-based prevalence survey with RT-PCR and whole-genome sequencing
datoms.notes: Study conducted during peak outbreak, limiting full characterization. Misclassification in identification of prior SARS-CoV-2 exposure using previous serosurveys.

dataQualityNote: All 45 datoms were retrieved via the Datomer's datom_ids array using batch-get-item, not the datomerId-createdAt-index GSI: each individual datom record's own datomerId field points to a different originating cluster than this claim's datomerId (060a045c...), so the GSI query returned 0 rows and cluster membership had to be resolved from the Datomer item's explicit datom_ids list instead. sourceJournal is empty on all 45 records (journal metadata was not populated at ingestion for this batch), so it is omitted from the source strings. 24 of 45 records are evidence_type TEXT_NO_METADATA (extracted from text without full structured source metadata) versus 21 PDF_FULL_TEXT. The two randomized-trial datoms both have sample_size recorded as "Not reported" in the source data. 25 of 45 records carry source_year 2026, reflecting genuinely recent 2026 publications (verified against real DOIs and PubMed URLs), not an ingestion artifact.
scope: Adults in the United States, Brazil, Germany, Singapore, India, and China, including older adults, dialysis patients, and people with weakened immune systems
metric: Risk of reinfection or hospitalization, antibody levels in the blood, and T-cell immune response to the virus
aboutClaim:
This claim is built on 45 real pieces of evidence, but DATOM only gives it a 31% confidence score, the "Preliminary" band, because the evidence is genuinely mixed. 20 pieces support the idea that hybrid immunity, having had both a prior infection and a vaccine, adds protection. 2 directly argue against it, and 23 only support it under certain conditions, like a person's age, whether they were on dialysis, or which variant was spreading at the time.

Only 2 of the 45 pieces of evidence are randomized controlled trials. Most of the support instead comes from observational studies that just tracked what happened to different groups of people, and for several of these, the number of people studied was simply not recorded.

The overall picture is real, but not clean. One large study followed 101,941 people and found a 26 to 36% drop in reinfection risk. But a study of 535 people in Salvador, Brazil found that a variant called BQ.1* still infected 56% of the population, even though about 97% of them already had some prior infection and/or vaccination.
